The four-day rise in the 10-year yield, at 27.5 basis points, is the most since April 2025. 

   And it has come without fresh news about inflation, growth, Fed tightening, budget deficits or AI borrowing.

   It may be time to review what Ben Chabot, a former Chicago Fed economist now teaching at Northwestern University and the University of Chicago, describes as, effectively, a run on the bond market. 

         Depositors worried about their bank may withdraw money out of fear others will beat them to it, and bank failure becomes self-fulfilling. The U.S. government cannot fail, and cannot be forced to buy back its bonds. Yet a failure of confidence can, in theory, generate behavior akin to a run on the bank.

   We think of markets converging to one steady state based on fundamentals like interest rates, economic growth, inflation and so on. Yet markets can polarize between totally different steady states. In the first, yields are low, governments can easily service their debts, investors don’t worry about others selling, so yields stay low. In the second, yields rise, governments face trouble servicing their debts, investors worry others will sell, so they sell first. Yields rise more.

   “In short, when the decision to hold bonds depends on other investors beliefs about what other investors will do, we get two states of the world,” Chabot wrote on his Substack . “These two equilibria are self-fulfilling. As soon as a critical mass of bondholders believe they are in a given equilibria their behavior assures that they are!”

   Is the U.S. moving from one state to another? There is no obvious sign of that yet, such as rising expected inflation, which would reflect fears the Fed will be pressured to keep rates low or buy the debt. But with U.S. (indeed, global) debts in uncharted territory, the possibility can’t be dismissed.

It is hard to say how much to chalk up to AI, rather than longer-running trends like the decline of newspapers, record sales and Hollywood blockbusters. Pulling together globe-spanning data on fertility declines, Coffey finds that “where and when fertility has fallen low, it has tended to keep falling .” Some demographers had been more optimistic, because low fertility rebounded in Northern Europe in the early 2000s. China, and many Western economists, say the accord didn’t work for Japan and won’t work for China now. For China, “the issue is not whether it will rebalance, but whether it will do so by shifting income and demand toward households, or by postponing the adjustment for a few more years through further accumulation of debt and excess capacity,” he writes.

Greg Ip
 
Could There Be a Run on the Bond Market?
 
Plus, AI and college grads, falling birthrates, and a historical lesson for the Chinese yuan
 

The rise in bond yields is starting to carry a whiff of fear. The four-day rise in the 10-year yield, at 27.5 basis points, is the most since April 2025. 

 

And it has come without fresh news about inflation, growth, Fed tightening, budget deficits or AI borrowing.

 

It may be time to review what Ben Chabot, a former Chicago Fed economist now teaching at Northwestern University and the University of Chicago, describes as, effectively, a run on the bond market. 

 
 
 
 

Depositors worried about their bank may withdraw money out of fear others will beat them to it, and bank failure becomes self-fulfilling. The U.S. government cannot fail, and cannot be forced to buy back its bonds. Yet a failure of confidence can, in theory, generate behavior akin to a run on the bank.

 

We think of markets converging to one steady state based on fundamentals like interest rates, economic growth, inflation and so on. Yet markets can polarize between totally different steady states. In the first, yields are low, governments can easily service their debts, investors don’t worry about others selling, so yields stay low. In the second, yields rise, governments face trouble servicing their debts, investors worry others will sell, so they sell first. Yields rise more.

 

“In short, when the decision to hold bonds depends on other investors beliefs about what other investors will do, we get two states of the world,” Chabot wrote on his Substack. “These two equilibria are self-fulfilling. As soon as a critical mass of bondholders believe they are in a given equilibria their behavior assures that they are!”

 

Is the U.S. moving from one state to another? There is no obvious sign of that yet, such as rising expected inflation, which would reflect fears the Fed will be pressured to keep rates low or buy the debt. But with U.S. (indeed, global) debts in uncharted territory, the possibility can’t be dismissed.

What I’m Following

 

AI hasn’t made it harder for young college grads to find work. So find UCLA economists Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu, who compared unemployment for early-20s college grads this past summer with past years. Joblessness for young grads is usually higher in the summer months. But even though more companies are adopting AI, unemployment for these workers didn’t climb higher this summer than it has in recent years. 

 

Nowhere are workers feeling the AI pressure more intensely than in the media business, where jobs have declined by more than 200,000, or roughly 15%, over the past four years, notes economics blogger Joseph Politano. It is hard to say how much to chalk up to AI, rather than longer-running trends like the decline of newspapers, record sales and Hollywood blockbusters. But as machine-learning tools gain stronger visual-arts capabilities and chatbots displace web browsing, media workers could face even more disruption.

 
 
 
 

The decline in global fertility has to level out at some point…right? Not so fast, write UT Austin’s Dianne Coffey and three co-authors. Pulling together globe-spanning data on fertility declines, Coffey finds that “where and when fertility has fallen low, it has tended to keep falling.” Some demographers had been more optimistic, because low fertility rebounded in Northern Europe in the early 2000s. But even there, more up-to-date numbers show fertility proceeded to decline further.

 

China’s enormous trade surpluses have led to calls for joint action to raise its currency, the yuan, akin to 1985’s Plaza Accord, which boosted an undervalued Japanese yen in order to reduce Japan’s trade surpluses. China, and many Western economists, say the accord didn’t work for Japan and won’t work for China now. But analysts often take the wrong lesson from that episode, Michael Pettis writes for the Carnegie Endowment. Yes, Japan’s economy stagnated in the decades that followed, but Pettis attributes that to a combination of misguided fiscal and monetary policy, not to the currency accord itself. For China, “the issue is not whether it will rebalance, but whether it will do so by shifting income and demand toward households, or by postponing the adjustment for a few more years through further accumulation of debt and excess capacity,” he writes.

• In a Pennsylvania town, $10,000 payments aren’t enough to persuade some residents to support allowing data-center construction.

 
 
 

What to Watch

• The BLS’s Jolts report will add detail on whether the low-hire, low-fire labor market persisted in August.

 

• Economists expect the Conference Board’s consumer-confidence index will decline to 89.2 in its September reading, from 89.4 in August.

 

Wednesday

 

• G-20 trade ministers gather in Milwaukee, one day after a U.S. import ban on Canadian motorcycles and other products takes effect.

 

• At 8:30 a.m. ET, the BEA publishes its third estimate of second-quarter GDP as well as August PCE numbers. Analysts think core prices likely rose by 0.3% in August, faster than July’s 0.2% and enough to raise 12-month core PCE inflation to 3.4%. Revisions and a formula tweak add uncertainty.
